passage: Abstract: "A frequent experimental flaw is the application of oversampling algorithms to the entire dataset, resulting in biased models and overly-optimistic estimates." (copying rows = random oversampling, L1.4 by PB's tie rule, SOURCES_D)
faulty: Random oversampling (minority rows copied with replacement until the classes have equal counts) is applied to all 400 records; stratified 5-fold cross-validation with an unpruned CART tree then runs on the enlarged data; sensitivity for the positive class, pooled over the test folds (which contain copies), is the statistic. Claim holds when sensitivity >= 0.60.
fixed: Stratified 5-fold cross-validation on the original 400 records; random oversampling of the training folds only; sensitivity on the original test-fold records, pooled.
estimand: Faulty: sensitivity on test rows that are copies of training rows. Fixed: sensitivity on new records.
model_family: Unpruned CART decision tree with random oversampling. Chosen by me: an unpruned tree reproduces a copied row exactly, so the copy leak is visible; the abstract names no classifier.
sizes_note: Source sizes: not stated in the abstract (full text not open). 400 x 8 is the small-sample regime; cheap. Dependence on the oversampling ratio: not stated.
exploited_structure: A small positive class whose rows are duplicated, so exact copies of test positives are in the training data.

structure_statistic.note_value_source: source states none: the abstract gives no imbalance ratio; 0.1 is a typical minority share proposed as the setting's value

notes: L1.4 (copying rows) by PB tie rule. The statistic comes from labels only, which a claim-false world keeps. Differs from B2B-03/04 in the pipeline step (duplication vs synthesis), statistic (sensitivity) and size.
